additionalPrimaryEvidence.text: bʌṭkumɑ̄̀r, -ah n.f. ‘a young (pubescent) girl (twelve to fourteen years old); a virgin’. A typical synonym compound basically meaning ‘girl-girl’. Second element (OIA kumārī́- [3303]) is not inherited but borrowed from one of the Dardic languages where OIA medial -m- is preserveḍ First element < *beṭṭa- (9238). Turner’s quote of Toṛ bat-kumā ‘maid’ sub vṛddhá-2 (12073) is, of course, wrong. Cf. below bɑ̄́ṭ-lakʌ̀y ‘children’ and the similar synonym compound Buṛ/Sh. ćumuṭkér ‘junge Frau’, Kho. and Kal. čhumuṭkēr ‘marriageable girl, maiden’, Wkh. čə;itk;ír ‘femme aux cheveux bouclés; vieille femme parée comme une jeune’ (also Gy. čhumut ‘beautiful girl’). Acc̣ to Berger < *choṭṭa- and kumārī́. However, this is a triple synonym compound: ﬁrst syllable cf. Kal. čhu ‘daughter’ (ﬁrst syllable < duhitŕ.- [6481], second syllable < *maṭṭa- [9723], and third syllable < kuḍa-1 [3245]); the different vowels in čhumuṭkēr are the result of (not uncommon) vowel leftshift and metaphony: at an intermediate stage *čhumaṭukuṛi the second -u- (a dimin. sufﬁx) shifted to the left, producing *čhumuṭkaṛi, and metaphony caused the present form of the ﬁnal vowel (cf. the different etymological interpretation of Bashir 2001: 11f.). Further similar compound formations are: Kam. j’ukuř ‘woman’ ( < duhitŕ.- and kuḍa-1), B dh́ï-bïō̃̀ ‘a woman’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-sister’), nā̃kvüṭ ‘a girl’ (liṭ: ‘wife-girl’), J dhižū́ ‘a daughter’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-daughter’), bng. beṭkuṛi ‘young daughter’ (liṭ: ‘daughter-girl’), Ash. istrimalī-kuṛɑ̈̄ ‘girl’ (a triple compound < strī́- plus mahallikā- plus kuḍa-1 [liṭ: ‘woman-mother-girl’]), and Kal. istrížagúa.k ‘young girl’ (a triple compound < strī́- plus jāyɑ̄́- plus kuḍa-1 [liṭ: ‘woman-wife-girl’]). This type of compound is apparently limited to the NW and to Munda: Sanṭ coṇḍ kuṛi ‘a girl from 8 to 10’ (liṭ: ‘girl-girl’).

Exact Shina component nodes with these meanings were not found: the existing muṭ/muṭh nodes mean fist, arm or shoulder and must not be substituted. Degener’s explicit Zoller cross-reference therefore remains a morphological research lead.
cases.primaryEvidenceText: mṹĩṭhʌṽ adv.; postp.; adj.; v.i. ‘ahead, in front; front; to be ahead’ (Uṛ āge honā, āge huā), cf. mũĩṭhrʌ́ṽ. Ex.: sùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ bḗth ‘he walks ahead; sùh tʌ̀s-mũĩṭhʌṽ bḗth (a) ‘he walks ahead of him’, (b) ‘he goes up to him’; sùh bhɑ̄̀-mũĩṭhʌṽ bhḕṭh thū̀ ‘he sits in front of the house’; sùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ bhɑ̄́-mʌz bhḕṭ thū̀ ‘he sits in the front house’; tùh mṹĩṭhʌṽ ‘be you ahead (of me), you are ahead of me, you (have) proceeded’. This last verbal use is to explained thus: as the etymological derivation below shows, this word (also in its function as a verb) is a derivation from a noun (resp. from the adverbial derivation of the noun). As a hab. verb its inﬁnitive and past participle have the same form in IK. Its use, however, is meanwhile reduced to just two functions, and even the place of the accent is “wrong”: in verbal use the accent normally had to be on the ﬁnal syllable. On the other hand, the -r- causative extension of the verb (see below) has a fully unfolded paradigm. The members of this lemma derive < OIA *mukhasthā-. The word mṹĩṭhʌṽ and its alloforms with the same ﬁnal syllable have an additional derivational sufﬁx. Woṭ. muṭh ‘vor’. Cf. J sāmùṭh and its similar etymology. Note that Sh. muc̣hṓ ‘in front’ does not directly correspond with the basic IK lemma but is an exact parallel to mṹĩṭh-nā̃ because the Sh. word can be decomposed into *muṭ plus ẓhō ‘from’.

cases.evidence: Degener barono ring compares Burushaski burondo and gives hatei barono finger-ring. The matching survey barono/barondo/borono forms preserve n/nd and rhotic differences. The comparison supports a contact family, but immediate donor identity and direction still require verification; do not merge this family with the finger-derived aŋg-/hag- names.

The aŋg-/hag- ring set invites comparison with aṅgulīya 136 and aṅguṣṭhiya 138, but its -l/-r and -sari extensions cannot all be treated as one inherited shape. Zoller pp. 63, 75 explicitly derives Indus Kohistani aṅguili ring from 136, while his aṅgṭhui belongs to 138; the Shina forms with h, velar weakening or -sari need their own correspondence or donor analysis. Preserve the two historical candidates and investigate the internal subgroups before assigning a common parent.

Degener bẽye both lacks an etymological attribution. Turner 6648 gives Shina du two and Sindhi bei both, but a b-initial parallel in another language is not sufficient to explain this Shina form, including its nasalization and ending. Zoller’s Kohistani duyaṽ/bhaždo/sab-du both expressions also do not establish the missing bridge; keep this form unassigned.

Degener c̣hīlo garment/clothing refers to Buddruss 1996 p. 42 without supplying a derivation. The survey’s c̣hīlo/c̣īle/ṣīle and cīlo forms provide a dialectal family, with initial articulation and adjective/noun endings retained, but a cīra rag connection has not been verified. In particular Turner 4844 concerns a splitting verb and explicitly marks its Shina affricate form as a loan; it is not direct evidence for these cloth nouns. The extended c̣hilīkhoi response needs component checking as well. Await the cited discussion before assigning a historical head.
